## Why This Is Asked

This tests precise bit-twiddling with non-trivial masks and no loops, a common optimization pattern.

## Key Concepts

- Mask construction for adjacent-bit swaps
- Two-shift strategy and one return
- Edge cases: 64-bit boundaries, unsigned masking

```c
uint64_t swapAdjacent64(uint64_t n) {
  const uint64_t E = 0x5555555555555555ULL;
  const uint64_t O = 0xAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAULL;
  return ((n & E) << 1) | ((n & O) >> 1);
}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tracks cross-word parity using SWAR folding without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Multi-word parity with bitwise folding
- SWAR technique to reduce 64-bit to 1 bit
- No loops or branches across 256 bits

## Code Example
```javascript
unsigned parity256(uint64_t a,uint64_t b,uint64_t c,uint64_t d){
  auto p64 = x => { x ^= x>>32; x ^= x>>16; x ^= x>>8; x ^= x>>4; x ^= x>>2; x ^= x>>1; return x & 1; };
  return p64(a) ^ p64(b) ^ p64(c) ^ p64(d);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- Extend to 512-bit input; how to minimize temp storage?
- Compare branchless parity to a popcount-based approach on modern CPUs.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to implement a rotation primitive with wrap-around using only shifts and masks, including masking to handle large r and the n=0 edge case.

## Key Concepts
- Circular shift using (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n))
- Masking r with 31 to confine to 0..31
- Edge-case n=0 preserves x exactly

## Code Example
```c
static inline uint32_t rotl32(uint32_t x, unsigned r) {
  unsigned n = r & 31; // 0..31
  return (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n));
}
```

- How would you generalize to 64-bit rotates?
- What are the potential performance differences vs. compiler intrinsics like _rotl?
- How would you test across boundary values (r=0, r=31, r=32, r=33)?

## Why This Is Asked
This tests the ability to implement a branchless, 64-bit rotate using masking and shifts—a fundamental low-level technique in performance-critical code.

## Key Concepts
- 64-bit masking with &63 to constrain the rotation range
- Branchless rotation via (n >> r) | (n << (64 - r))
- Edge-case handling for k=0 without conditional branches

## Code Example
```javascript
function rotateRight64(n, k) {
  const r = k & 63;
  return (n >>> r) | (n << ((64 - r) & 63));
}
```

- How would this implementation behave on architectures with native rotate instructions?
